intro:
These exercises turn the chapter's four primitives, move, share, synchronize, and borrow-in-scope, into design judgment. Each one asks you to read ownership at a thread boundary rather than reach for whatever compiled first. The warm-ups make Send and Sync concrete; the implementation and debugging work force you to put owned data on the correct side of `thread::spawn`; and the design scenarios make you commit to a concurrency model and name its operational cost.

The throughline is that Rust's thread safety is not a separate subsystem bolted onto the language. It is the same ownership and borrowing model from Chapter 04, extended across an OS-thread boundary by two marker traits. Once you can say where the mutable state lives and who is allowed to touch it, the choice between a channel, an `Arc<Mutex<T>>`, and a scoped thread stops being a syntax preference and becomes a statement about the design.

exerciseSolutions.title: Decide whether a type is Send, Sync, both, or neither
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Fix the definitions first. `Send` means a value of the type can be moved to another thread and used there safely as an owned value; ownership transfers across the thread boundary. `Sync` means it is safe for multiple threads to hold shared references (`&T`) to the same value at once; equivalently, `T: Sync` exactly when `&T: Send`. Both are auto traits: the compiler derives them for a type when all of its fields qualify, and the entire point is that a type which fails to qualify will not compile its way across `thread::spawn`.

Now classify. `String` is both `Send` and `Sync`: it owns a heap buffer with no shared mutable interior, so moving it to a thread is fine and a `&String` shared across threads is read-only and safe. `Arc<String>` is also `Send` and `Sync`: `Arc` uses atomic reference counting, so cloning the handle from several threads cannot corrupt the count, and the inner `String` is itself immutable through the shared `Arc`. `Mutex<Vec<u8>>` is `Send` and `Sync`: the lock serializes access, so even though the `Vec` is mutated, only one thread holds the guard at a time, which is the whole reason `Mutex` exists.

The two that are not safe to share are instructive. `Rc<String>` is neither `Send` nor `Sync`, because its reference count is a plain non-atomic integer; two threads cloning or dropping the same `Rc` would race on that counter and could free the allocation twice. `RefCell<Vec<u8>>` is `Send` (you can move it) but not `Sync`, because its borrow flag is a non-atomic cell, so concurrent `borrow_mut` calls from two threads would not be detected and would alias mutably. That is why `Rc<RefCell<T>>` is the canonical single-thread sharing tool and never crosses a thread boundary, whereas `Arc<Mutex<T>>` is its multi-thread counterpart, not a synonym for it.

The raw-pointer wrapper is the case that demands restraint. A struct holding a `*mut T` is `!Send` and `!Sync` by default because the compiler cannot see what the pointer aliases or who else mutates through it. Reaching for `unsafe impl Send`/`unsafe impl Sync` is only correct if you can actually prove the hidden aliasing, mutation, and destruction behavior is thread-safe; the keyword is a promise to the compiler, not an escape hatch, and most application code should never write it.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Compile-time assertions that pin down which standard types are Send and/or Sync.
criteria: Both traits are defined before any example is classified: Send is move-to-thread, Sync is shared-reference-across-threads (&T: Send).
Rc<String> is identified as neither Send nor Sync because its refcount is non-atomic, ruling out transfer and sharing.
Arc<String> (Send + Sync, immutable inner) is kept distinct from Arc<Mutex<T>> (lock required for mutation).
The raw-pointer wrapper is flagged as !Send/!Sync until an explicit safety proof justifies an unsafe auto-trait impl.

exerciseSolutions.title: Compare a channel-based design with a shared-state design
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Start by asking where the mutable state really lives. In the channel design (the chapter's Example 1), each worker owns its job batch outright: the `Vec<Job>` is moved into the worker by the `move` closure, the worker computes a total over data nobody else can touch, and it sends a small owned tuple back over `mpsc`. The only thread that ever mutates the result map is the main thread, draining `rx`. Mutation authority is singular and the ownership flow is one-directional. In the shared-state design (Example 2), the mutable state lives behind `Arc<Mutex<HashMap<...>>>`: `Arc` makes the one allocation reachable from every thread, and every worker locks, mutates the shared map directly, and unlocks. Mutation authority is shared and arbitrated by the lock at runtime.

Message passing keeps one thread as the owner of mutation. Its operational win is failure visibility and order: results arrive as discrete messages, the aggregation point is explicit and deterministic, and a backed-up consumer shows up as channel backlog rather than as a corrupted structure. Its operational cost is buffering and backpressure, an unbounded channel can grow without limit if producers outrun the consumer, and a bounded channel forces you to decide what happens when it is full (block, drop, or error). It is the calmer model when message order matters, because the receiver sees a defined sequence rather than the interleaving of many concurrent writers.

Shared-state locking makes contention and lock scope the main runtime risk. Its operational win is that it is the honest model when many threads genuinely need to observe and update the same structure: there is exactly one copy of the data, every thread sees the latest committed state, and you avoid copying large structures through messages. Its operational cost is contention, the wider the critical section, the more threads serialize on that one lock, and lock wait time becomes a real, measurable latency source; you also inherit poisoning semantics if a thread panics while holding the guard. It is the calmer model precisely when the data is one shared thing that everyone must read and write, not a stream of results to be folded together.

Neither model is globally superior. The right call follows the workload: a worker-result pipeline where each producer owns its inputs and only the aggregator writes is a natural fit for channels; a hot shared counter table that every request thread must update in place is a natural fit for `Arc<Mutex<T>>` (or a sharded/atomic variant). The design smell is choosing one because it resembles a pattern from another language rather than because the ownership story actually demands it.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Two shapes side by side: owned inputs plus channel aggregation versus one locked shared map.
criteria: Ownership and mutation authority are stated for both: workers own their inputs in the channel design; the map is shared behind Arc<Mutex> in the other.
Message passing gets one win (deterministic, visible aggregation/order) and one cost (channel backlog/backpressure).
Shared-state locking gets one win (single source of truth all threads update) and one cost (lock contention and wait time).
The answer refuses a global winner and ties each model to the workload that suits it.

exerciseSolutions.title: Move owned jobs into worker threads and report totals
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The design is the chapter's Example 1 shape: two real OS threads, each the sole owner of its job batch, publishing results back through a channel. The key decisions are all about ownership at the boundary. The worker closure must be a `move` closure so that the `Vec<Job>` and the cloned `Sender` are transferred into the child thread rather than borrowed from the parent stack; if you borrowed instead, the child could outlive the borrowed data and the compiler would reject it. Keeping the input owned, rather than passing a `&[Job]` slice into `thread::spawn`, is what lets each worker run independently with no lifetime tie back to `main`.

Results travel as small owned `(&'static str, u32)` tuples over `mpsc`. This is the deliberate channel-first choice: no worker touches a shared result map, so there is no lock, no contention, and no shared mutability to reason about. Each worker computes its own total with `jobs.iter().map(|j| j.cost).sum()` over data nobody else can see, then sends one message. Because the worker is the sole owner while it runs, this is a clean ownership story end to end.

The caller joins both handles explicitly before treating the result as complete. Joining is where failure from a child thread becomes visible to the parent: a panicked worker surfaces as an `Err` from `join`, and joining also guarantees the worker has finished and dropped its `Sender` clone. Once both senders (the two clones) are dropped, the `for (worker, total) in rx` loop terminates naturally, because the receiver iterator ends when all senders are gone. The aggregation, summing per-worker totals into a grand total, happens on the single main thread, which keeps the final fold deterministic.

This is exactly the lab. Running it with `ingest` jobs of cost 2 and 3 and an `index` job of cost 4 prints `ingest = 5`, `index = 4`, `grand = 9`.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Each worker owns its Vec<Job> via a move closure and reports its total through mpsc.
criteria: Each worker closure owns its input: the Vec<Job> is consumed by a move closure, not borrowed.
Results flow through an mpsc channel; no worker writes a shared mutable map directly.
The caller joins both handles explicitly before draining the channel.
Output is ingest = 5, index = 4, grand = 9, matching the lab's expected ingest/index/grand totals.

exerciseSolutions.title: Repair a thread boundary that captures the wrong thing
exerciseSolutions.solution:
There are two distinct defects, and they want different repairs because their lifetime and ownership stories differ.

Defect one: a function borrows a stack-local slice into `thread::spawn`. `thread::spawn` requires its closure to be `'static`, because the spawned thread may outlive the current stack frame; a `&[T]` pointing at a parent local does not satisfy that bound, so the borrow is rejected. There are two correct repairs depending on intent. If the worker genuinely needs to own the data and survive independently, move owned data in: take a `Vec<T>` (or `to_vec()` the slice) and capture it with a `move` closure, the calm default for request-local job data. If, instead, the work is short-lived and finishes before the function returns, the data does not need to be cloned at all: use `thread::scope`, whose child threads are guaranteed to be joined at the end of the scope, so the compiler permits them to borrow parent-owned data directly. Prefer the scoped repair when the child cannot outlive the parent, it avoids needless allocation and keeps the borrow honest.

Defect two: a function tries to send `Rc<RefCell<State>>` into a thread. This fails to compile because `Rc<T>` is `!Send` (its reference count is non-atomic and would race across threads) and `RefCell<T>` is `!Sync` (its borrow flag is non-atomic, so concurrent borrows would alias mutably undetected). The fix is not to paper over it with `unsafe`; it is to choose the shape that matches what the state actually is. If the state is genuinely shared and mutated by multiple threads, replace it with `Arc<Mutex<State>>`: `Arc` gives thread-safe shared ownership via atomic counts, and `Mutex` serializes mutation so only one thread holds the guard at a time. But justify that on semantics, not on the compiler complaining: if only one thread should really own and mutate the state, the better refactor is message passing, send owned commands to a single owner thread over a channel and let that thread be the sole mutator, which removes the lock entirely and gives one clear owner per mutable subsystem.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Four repairs: scoped borrow, owned move, Arc<Mutex> for real sharing, and channel to a single owner.
criteria: At least one case is repaired by moving owned data into the child via a move closure (sum_owned).
At least one case is repaired with thread::scope so borrowed local data needs no clone (sum_slice_scoped).
Rc<RefCell<T>> is explained as the wrong cross-thread shape: Rc is !Send (non-atomic count), RefCell is !Sync (non-atomic borrow flag).
The Arc<Mutex<T>> repair is justified semantically (state genuinely shared and mutated), with message passing offered when one owner suffices.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose channel-based or shared-state concurrency for a service
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Map the pipeline `accept -> parse -> schedule -> update metrics -> publish completion` to the model that makes ownership calmest under load, and let a service use more than one model where each subsystem warrants it.

Channel-based boundaries: the request lifecycle itself moves as owned messages. After `accept` and `parse`, each request becomes an owned work item that is sent over a channel into the scheduling stage and on to a worker pool; the CPU-heavy job runs on a worker that owns its input alone. Completion is published the same way, the worker sends an owned completion record back to a publisher thread rather than mutating a shared completion structure. The justification is that these stages have a natural single owner at each step and care about ordering and backpressure: a backed-up worker pool shows up as growing queue depth, a signal you can act on, instead of silent contention. A bounded channel here is deliberate, it lets the service apply backpressure (block or shed load) when producers outrun workers.

Immutable shared state through `Arc<T>` only: configuration, routing tables, parsing schemas, and any reference data loaded at startup and never mutated should be shared as `Arc<Config>`. Every thread holds a cheap cloned handle to one allocation, reads are lock-free, and there is no mutation to coordinate. The justification is that this data is read by everyone and written by no one during request handling, which is exactly the case `Arc<T>` without a lock is for.

Synchronized mutable shared state: the few hot counters and the one central retry table are the honest place for synchronized shared state, but only because they are genuinely shared ownership, not convenience. The retry table must be observed and updated by many request threads (a retry recorded by one thread must be visible to another that picks the work up), so a single shared structure is the correct semantics. For the hot counters, prefer atomics or sharded counters to keep the critical section tiny; for the retry table, an `Arc<Mutex<RetryTable>>` (or a concurrent map) is defensible, with the lock scope kept as narrow as a single entry update. If a counter could instead be owned by one aggregator thread fed by channel messages, that is often calmer, push the design toward one owner per mutable subsystem.

Observability hooks: monitor queue depth on the work channels (the primary backpressure signal), lock wait time on the retry-table mutex (rising wait time means contention is becoming your latency), and worker panic count from join results (a crashed worker should be counted and replaced, not silently lost). Together these tell you whether the bottleneck is throughput, contention, or failure.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Each subsystem mapped to its model: bounded channel, Arc-only config, atomic counter, locked retry table.
criteria: At least one channel-based boundary is chosen and justified: request lifecycle moves as owned messages with backpressure as the signal.
At least one immutable shared-state boundary uses Arc<T> alone: startup config/routing data read by all, written by none.
Mutable shared state (retry table, hot counters) is justified by real shared ownership, with atomics/narrow locks preferred over convenience.
Observability hooks are named: queue depth, mutex lock wait time, and worker panic count.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose OS threads, scoped threads, work stealing, async tasks, or distributed workers
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The four workloads map to four different execution models, and the discipline is keeping them separate rather than blurring them under the word 'concurrency'.

The request-local slice transform wants scoped OS threads. The data is a slice owned by the parent stack frame, the work is brief, and the child threads will finish before the function returns. `thread::scope` is built for exactly this: it guarantees its spawned threads are joined at the end of the scope, so they may borrow parent-owned data directly without `'static` bounds, cloning, or heap-sharing. Choosing scoped threads here avoids copying the slice just to satisfy `thread::spawn`'s lifetime requirement.

The large CPU-bound collection map wants a work-stealing, data-parallel scheduler (Rayon-style). The chunk sizes may be uneven, so a fixed hand-partitioning into N `thread::spawn` calls would leave some threads idle while others grind through heavy chunks. A work-stealing pool keeps all cores busy by letting idle workers steal pending chunks from busy ones, and it amortizes thread creation across a fixed pool. This is a scheduler strategy layered over OS threads, not a different kind of thread, the win is load balancing under uneven work, expressed as something close to a parallel iterator.

The network fan-out with many waiting sockets is an async-task problem, not an OS-thread problem. Each connection spends almost all its time waiting on IO, so spawning one OS thread per socket spends real memory and scheduler attention on threads that are merely parked. An async executor multiplexes thousands of waiting tasks onto a small thread pool, suspending each task at its await points instead of blocking a thread. The mistake to avoid is 'solving waiting with more threads', waiting is what async IO is for.

The job that must run on another machine is no longer a multithreading problem at all; it is a distributed-systems problem. Crossing the network boundary changes the ownership and failure model completely: there is no shared address space, no `Send` to lean on, messages can be lost or duplicated, and the remote worker can fail independently. It belongs behind an RPC or a durable queue with explicit serialization, timeouts, retries, and idempotency, and calling it 'multithreading' hides exactly the failure modes that distinguish it. Keep OS threads, async tasks, and distributed workers in three separate mental buckets.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One model per workload: scoped threads, a work-stealing pool, async tasks, and a distributed queue.
criteria: OS threads, async tasks, and distributed workers are kept in three clearly separate categories.
Scoped threads are chosen for the borrowed local CPU-bound transform, avoiding needless cloning.
A work-stealing/data-parallel model is chosen for the uneven CPU-bound collection map to balance load.
Network fan-out is explained as an async-task problem (parked IO waits multiplexed) rather than a thread-per-socket spray, and the cross-machine job is named distributed, not multithreaded.

labSolution.explanation:
The starter code had two defects: the worker closure was not a `move` closure (so it could not own `jobs` or `tx`), and it hard-coded `let total = 0` instead of summing the job costs. The fix is to make the closure `move` (transferring ownership of the `Vec<Job>` and the cloned `Sender` into the child thread) and to compute the real total with `jobs.iter().map(|job| job.cost).sum()`. Because each worker owns its batch outright, no lock or shared map is needed; results travel back as small owned `(&'static str, u32)` tuples over the `mpsc` channel.

Ownership flows in one direction. `main` clones the sender once so both workers can publish, then moves each owned job vector into its worker. The `ingest` worker sums 2 + 3 = 5; the `index` worker sums 4 = 4. After both workers are joined (which also makes any worker panic visible and guarantees both `Sender` clones are dropped), the `for (worker, total) in rx` loop drains the channel; the loop terminates naturally once all senders are gone. The main thread accumulates the grand total 5 + 4 = 9 while recording each per-worker total, then prints `ingest = 5`, `index = 4`, `grand = 9`.

This is the channel-first design from the chapter's Example 1: one owner per mutable piece of state, message passing for results, and a single deterministic aggregation point on the main thread.

reviewAnswers.question: What does `Send` mean, and what does `Sync` mean?
reviewAnswers.answer: `Send` means a value of the type can be moved to another thread and safely used there as an owned value, so ownership can cross the thread boundary. `Sync` means it is safe for multiple threads to hold shared references (`&T`) to the same value simultaneously; formally, `T: Sync` exactly when `&T: Send`. Both are auto traits with no methods that the compiler derives automatically when all of a type's fields qualify, and they are the entire mechanism behind 'data races do not compile'.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is a `move` closure the ordinary shape for `thread::spawn`?
reviewAnswers.answer: `thread::spawn` requires its closure to be `'static`, because the spawned thread may outlive the stack frame that created it, so the closure cannot hold short-lived borrows of parent locals. A `move` closure transfers ownership of the captured non-Copy values (job batches, owned buffers, request-local data) into the child thread, giving the child data that survives independently. That is why `move` is the calm default: it puts the owned data on the correct side of the boundary instead of leaving the child pointing at a frame that may already be gone.

reviewAnswers.question: When is `thread::scope` a better answer than cloning or heap-sharing more data?
reviewAnswers.answer: `thread::scope` is better when the worker only needs to borrow parent-owned data briefly and is guaranteed to finish before the parent continues. The scope joins all of its spawned threads at the end of the block, so the compiler permits them to borrow parent-owned data directly without a `'static` bound. That lets you avoid cloning the data or wrapping it in `Arc` purely to satisfy `thread::spawn`'s lifetime requirement, which is the right call whenever the child cannot outlive the parent.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the difference between message passing and shared-state locking as an ownership design?
reviewAnswers.answer: Message passing keeps one thread as the owner of a piece of mutable state: other threads send it owned commands or results over a channel, and only that one thread mutates, so the aggregation point is explicit and ordering is deterministic. Shared-state locking instead gives many threads access to one allocation (via `Arc`) and arbitrates their mutations with a lock (`Mutex`), so authority over the data is shared and serialized at runtime. The first trades buffering and backpressure for a single clear owner; the second trades lock contention for a genuine single source of truth that every thread reads and writes.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is work stealing a scheduler strategy rather than a synonym for threads?
reviewAnswers.answer: Work stealing is how a fixed pool of worker threads is scheduled, not a different kind of thread. Each worker keeps a queue of tasks, and when a worker runs out it steals pending tasks from a busy worker's queue, which keeps all cores busy when chunk sizes are uneven. The threads underneath are ordinary OS threads; work stealing is the load-balancing policy layered on top, which is why a Rayon-style pool is often calmer than hand-rolling many `thread::spawn` calls for CPU-bound collection work.

reviewAnswers.question: Why are async tasks and distributed workers separate from OS-thread design even when all three are 'concurrent'?
reviewAnswers.answer: OS threads are scheduled by the operating system and cost real memory and scheduler attention, so they suit CPU-bound work. Async tasks are scheduled by an executor and suspend at await points instead of blocking, so they suit IO-bound waiting where thousands of parked tasks can multiplex onto a few threads; solving waiting with more OS threads is the classic mismatch. Distributed workers cross a network boundary, which changes the ownership and failure model entirely, no shared address space, messages that can be lost or duplicated, independent failure, so they belong behind RPC or durable queues with timeouts and retries, not under the label 'multithreading'.
